The chapter says the number of international tourists in India is constantly growing, and that the increase after 2010 is especially marked and consistent. Foreign tourists visit India for heritage, adventure, cultural, health and business tourism, and ecotourism is also being given a boost.

Considering the heritage of India there are plenty of opportunities for tourism in many parts of the country, and many places are being developed for it. India's natural diversity — its mountains, coasts, forests and varied climate — is what makes so many different kinds of tourism possible in one country, so the future of tourism in India is indeed bright.

Right.

In ordinary trade goods are carried out of a country and their movement can be seen and counted. In tourism nothing leaves the country: the tourist comes to it and spends there, on travel, stay, food, guides and souvenirs, and the country earns foreign exchange from that spending.

Because the earning is real but no goods cross the border, tourism is called an invisible trade. The chapter treats it as an economic activity of exactly this kind — it calls tourism an important economic activity and measures it by the number of international tourists a country receives.

Right.

The chapter states it in those words: the development of means of transport is an indicator of rapid progress of a country.

The comparison in the chapter shows why. India has a denser network of transport than Brazil; about 85 per cent of passenger and 70 per cent of freight traffic are carried by roads every year, and railways are important for the growth of the Indian economy and are very important for a vast country where distances are large. In Brazil, by contrast, the forested lands of the Amazon River basin and the swampy lands have limited the development of roadways, railways have not developed well, and the contribution of airways is small — and those are the parts of the country that are least developed in every other way too.

Wrong.

Corrected sentence: India's time is ahead of Brazil's time.

The official Brazilian time, BRT, is the GMT−03 time zone, which is 3 hours BEHIND GMT. Indian Standard Time is taken from the 82.5° E longitude and is 5 hours 30 minutes AHEAD of GMT.

So India is 8 hours 30 minutes ahead of Brazil, not behind it. Brazil lies west of the 0° Meridian and India east of it, and places to the east always have the later time.

Wrong.

Corrected sentence: Tourism in India is very old; what has grown recently is the number of international tourists.

The chapter says that considering the HERITAGE of India there are plenty of opportunities for tourism in many parts of the country, and that foreign tourists come for heritage, adventure, cultural, health and business tourism. Heritage tourism of that kind rests on places that have drawn visitors and pilgrims for centuries.

What the chapter does describe as recent is the growth in numbers: the number of international tourists in India is constantly growing and the increase appears to be greater after 2010. Many places are also being newly developed for tourism. But the activity itself did not begin recently.

Brazil's attractions are chiefly natural, together with a few great cities.

Its forests and the wild animals in them attract many international tourists — Brazil has the largest number of vegetation species in the world and a greater diversity of wildlife than any other country, so the Amazon rainforest is a draw in itself. Its long coastline of about 7,400 km gives it a great many beaches, and its natural beauty is a tourist attraction in its own right.

Cities such as Rio de Janeiro attract tourists too, and the chapter notes that eco-tourism is being developed there.

So the factors are the rainforest and its wildlife, the beaches and coastal scenery, the natural beauty of the country and its famous cities.

The chapter says railways have not developed very well in Brazil, and that the use of trains for long-distance transport of passengers is restricted to a few urban tourist routes even though it is cheaper.

The difficulties in the interior are the same ones that have limited roads there: the forested lands of the Amazon River basin and the swampy lands. Laying a railway line through dense equatorial rainforest and marsh is very costly and very difficult to maintain, and the ground floods.

On top of that the interior is thinly peopled — the Amazon basin is very sparsely populated and settlements occur in only a few places — so there is little traffic to carry and the line could not pay for itself. Roadways, which account for more than half of Brazil's transport, are concentrated in the eastern part of the country for the same reasons.

Mobile telephones.

The chapter says that over recent years mobile telephones have led the rapid expansion of telecommunication services in Brazil. Today more than 45 per cent of the Brazilian population has access to the internet, and the telecommunications industry there includes landlines, mobile services, television and radio broadcasting and computer or internet access.

A mobile network needs no line laid to every house, so it can reach places that wires cannot — which matters in a country where, as the chapter says, the size of the land mass and the large pockets of unpopulated and densely vegetated areas are significant impediments to extending coverage.

The plane leaves Brasilia at 11:00 a.m. on Sunday, 31st December.

**Step 1 — find GMT.** The official Brazilian time, BRT, is the GMT−03 zone, that is 3 hours behind GMT.
GMT = 11:00 a.m. + 3 hours = **2:00 p.m., 31st December, Sunday.**

**Step 2 — New Delhi.** Indian Standard Time is taken from the 82.5° E longitude and is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.
Local time = 2:00 p.m. + 5 hours 30 minutes = **7:30 p.m., 31st December, Sunday.**

**Step 3 — Vladivostok.** The diagram places Vladivostok on about the 135° E meridian. 135 ÷ 15 = 9, so its standard time is 9 hours ahead of GMT.
Local time = 2:00 p.m. + 9 hours = **11:00 p.m., 31st December, Sunday.**

So when the plane leaves Brasilia it is 7:30 p.m. at New Delhi and 11:00 p.m. at Vladivostok, and at both places it is still Sunday, 31st December. Both are ahead of Brasilia because both lie east of it — India by 8 hours 30 minutes and Vladivostok by 12 hours.

[Note: the chapter gives BRT as GMT−03 and IST as 82.5° E, but it does not give a time zone for Vladivostok; the 135° E used above is read off the longitude scale of the printed diagram.]

| 'A' Group | 'B' Group |
|---|---|
| (a) Trans-Amazonian | (iv) Major Highways |
| (b) Road Transport | (iii) Golden Quadrilateral |
| (c) Rio de Janeiro | (i) Tourist Place |
| (d) Manmad | (ii) Railway Station in India |

The Trans-Amazonian is the highway that shows prominently on the transport map of Brazil, so it belongs with the major highways. The Golden Quadrilateral is India's great road project joining its four largest cities, so it goes with road transport. Rio de Janeiro is named in the chapter as one of the cities of Brazil that attract tourists. Manmad is a railway station in India.

Item (v), the 40° W. Meridian, is left over — it has no pair in the 'A' group.

[Note: item (i) is printed as 'Tourist Place Highway'. The word 'Highway' appears to have strayed from item (iv) 'Major Highways' in typesetting; the entry that matches Rio de Janeiro is 'Tourist Place'.]

Eco-tourism means travel to see and enjoy natural surroundings without spoiling them, so it can only be developed where there is a great deal of nature to see.

Brazil has exactly that. Its forests and the wild animals in them attract many international tourists; it has the largest number of vegetation species in the world and a greater diversity of wildlife than any other country; the Amazon rainforest, called the 'lungs of the world', covers its whole north; and it has a coastline of about 7,400 km with a great many beaches.

At the same time those forests are being degraded by slash-and-burn agriculture, deforestation and pollution. Eco-tourism gives an income that depends on the forest being kept standing rather than cleared, so developing it is a way of protecting what draws the visitors in the first place.

Brazil has great rivers, and the chapter says waterways have been developed on a commercial basis in the Amazon, where boats ply from Equitos in Peru to the mouth of the river — around 3,700 km, the longest waterway in the world that can be navigated. The south-flowing Parana is another important river for waterways, and coastal shipping is carried on along the coast.

What limits them is where those rivers run. The Amazon flows through the interior, which is very sparsely populated, covered by dense rainforest and swamp, and has almost no roads or railways to feed traffic to the river. A waterway is only useful if there are people and goods at both ends, and in the Amazon basin there are few of either — the chapter notes elsewhere that even the fish of the Amazon are not exploited much.

Meanwhile the population and the industry of Brazil are concentrated on the eastern coastal plain, away from the great rivers, and there roadways — which account for more than half of the country's transport — carry the traffic instead.

The chapter says the railway network in India is relatively less dense in the hill states, the north-eastern states, the central parts of India and Rajasthan, while it is dense in the North Indian Plains.

The plains suit railways in every way. The land is flat and level, so lines can be laid cheaply and straight, without tunnels, steep gradients or heavy bridging. The plains are also the most densely populated part of the country and the most intensively farmed, so there are many passengers to carry and a great deal of freight — grain, goods and raw materials — moving between the towns and cities strung along them.

Where the land is hilly, forested or desert, and where few people live, neither of those conditions holds, and the network there stays thin.

The chapter says plainly that the development of means of transport is an indicator of rapid progress of a country.

Transport is what lets the rest of the economy work. Raw materials must reach the factory and goods must reach the market; in India about 85 per cent of passenger and 70 per cent of freight traffic are carried by roads every year, and freight and passenger transport has been facilitated by the development of the railways, which the chapter calls important for the growth of the Indian economy. Railways matter especially for a vast country where distances are large.

Transport also carries people to work, to school and to hospital, and opens up regions that were cut off. Where it is missing, development stops: in Brazil the forested lands of the Amazon basin and the swampy lands have limited the building of roads, and those are the least developed parts of the country.

The chapter says that approximately 95 per cent of India's foreign trade moves through ocean routes.

Sea transport is used for international trade because it is by far the cheapest way of moving heavy and bulky goods over long distances. A ship can carry an enormous load in one journey, which no road vehicle, train or aircraft can match, and the ocean needs no track or road to be built and maintained. Most of the world's trading nations can be reached directly by sea.

India is well placed for it, with a long coastline and ports on both its western and eastern sides. The chapter adds that apart from international trade these routes are also used for transport between the islands and the rest of the country.

**Water transport in the Amazon.** It is well developed as a waterway. Waterways have been developed on a commercial basis in the Amazon; boats ply from Equitos in Peru right down to the mouth of the river, a distance of around 3,700 km, which the chapter calls the longest waterway in the world that can be navigated. The river is wide and deep enough for this along its whole course. But it runs through country that is very sparsely populated and covered by dense forest, so the traffic it carries is small, and it is not linked to a network of roads and railways.

**Water transport in the Ganga.** Waterways as a whole contribute only about 1 per cent of India's transport, and that share includes rivers, canals, backwaters and creeks together. The Ganga runs through the most densely populated and most intensively farmed part of India, so there is no shortage of goods or passengers — but that same plain carries a dense network of railways and roads, which take almost all the traffic. Its flow is also seasonal, being fed by the monsoon.

So the Amazon is a great navigable river with little traffic to carry, while the Ganga passes through crowded country but carries little because faster land transport is available beside it.

**Brazil.** Telecommunication services are well developed and efficient. The industry includes landlines, mobile services, television broadcasting, radio broadcasting and computer or internet access, and more than 45 per cent of the population has access to the internet. The infrastructure is fairly modern, particularly in central-south Brazil, but the north and north-west are drastically less developed. Over recent years mobile telephones have led the rapid expansion of services. The nature of Brazilian territory — the size of the land mass and the large pockets of unpopulated and densely vegetated areas — creates significant impediments to extending coverage. Brazil is also developing technology to send domestically-made satellites into space with its own rockets.

**India.** India has a denser network of transport and communication than Brazil, and its internal airways and other services are growing.

**In common.** In both countries the service is good where the people are and thin where they are not, and in both it is the mobile telephone that has spread fastest.

[Note: the chapter's account of communication in Brazil is much fuller than its account of communication in India, so the Indian side above is briefer than the Brazilian one.]

**IST — Indian Standard Time.** It is taken from the 82.5° E longitude, which passes through the middle of the country, and it is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT. India has only ONE standard time zone, although the difference between its two extreme longitudes is 2 hours or 120 minutes.

**BRT — Brazilian Standard Time.** The official Brazilian time is the GMT−03 zone, that is 3 hours BEHIND GMT. Brazil has FOUR time zones, being behind GMT by 2, 3, 4 or 5 hours depending on the part of the country.

So the two differ in three ways: India's is ahead of GMT and Brazil's behind it; India keeps one time for the whole country while Brazil keeps four; and India is 8 hours 30 minutes ahead of the official Brazilian time.

Modern means of communication carry information rather than goods, and they have grown very fast.

The chapter's account of Brazil lists what they are: landlines, mobile services, television broadcasting, radio broadcasting, and computer or internet access. Over recent years mobile telephones have led the rapid expansion of telecommunication services, and today more than 45 per cent of the Brazilian population has access to the internet.

Satellites are the newest of them. Brazil is developing technology to send domestically-made satellites into space with its own rockets.

Their reach depends on the country they must cross. Brazil's telecommunications infrastructure is fairly modern, particularly in central-south Brazil, while the north and north-west are drastically less developed, because the size of the land mass and the large pockets of unpopulated and densely vegetated areas are significant impediments to extending coverage.

Air transport is the fastest means of transport, and it can cross country that no road or railway can.

The chapter says that as compared to Brazil, airways in India are more developed, and that the use of internal airways is also increasing. In Brazil, by contrast, the contribution of airways to the transport system is small.

Air transport matters particularly in a vast country where distances are large, and it is the only quick way of reaching hilly and remote regions — the very areas where the chapter says the railway network is relatively less dense: the hill states, the north-eastern states, the central parts of India and Rajasthan. It also carries international passengers, on which India's growing tourist traffic depends.

[Note: the chapter does not name India's airports or give figures for its air traffic, so this note is confined to what it does say.]

Internal waterways can only exist where the physiography allows a river to be navigated, so the two are closely tied.

A waterway needs a river that is wide, deep and gently flowing over a long distance. The Amazon has exactly that: it crosses a vast level plain, so boats ply from Equitos in Peru to the mouth of the river, around 3,700 km, the longest navigable waterway in the world. The Parana, flowing south across the lowlands, is another river important for waterways in Brazil.

Where the land is high and broken a river cannot serve as a waterway, because rapids and waterfalls break the route and no boat can pass them. That is why Brazil's navigable waterways are the Amazon and the south-flowing Parana, both crossing lowlands, rather than the rivers of its highlands. In India waterways contribute only about 1 per cent of the country's transport, and that share is made up of rivers, canals, backwaters and creeks together.

Coasts matter too: a long, sheltered coastline permits coastal shipping, which is carried on in the coastal areas of Brazil, and India's coast lets about 95 per cent of its foreign trade move by ocean routes.

As the earth rotates, the sun is overhead at different places at different moments, so every meridian has its own local time. In a country with a large longitudinal extent that would mean many different clock times at once: the difference between India's two extreme points is 2 hours or 120 minutes, and Brazil's extremes lie further apart still.

A country therefore chooses one meridian and keeps its time for the whole country, or for a whole zone. India takes the 82.5° E longitude, which passes through the middle of the country, as Indian Standard Time, 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT, and keeps a single time zone. Brazil is so wide that it keeps four zones, behind GMT by 2, 3, 4 or 5 hours, of which GMT−03 is the official Brazilian time.

Standard time matters because everything that must be arranged in advance depends on it — railway and airline timetables, offices, schools, broadcasts, and trade and communication with other countries. Without it no two towns could agree on when anything was to happen.
